hints: Look at where cell Q is sitting and its shape - it is free in the middle of the capillary lumen and has a dark, pinched-in, biconcave appearance with no nucleus visible.
walkthrough:
Link Location to Cell Type**
You are looking inside a blood capillary in transverse section. The large pale space is the lumen, and the only free cells normally flowing through there are blood cells. Cell Q is the dark biconcave disc in the centre.

Recognise the Red Blood Cell**
That biconcave disc shape with no nucleus is classic for a mammalian red blood cell. It is packed with haemoglobin, which makes it electron-dense and dark in the micrograph, ideal for squeezing through narrow capillaries and carrying oxygen.
Final answer: red blood cell / erythrocyte

hints: Start by naming fluid R - it is the fluid bathing the respiring cells outside the capillary, formed when high blood pressure squeezes fluid out of the capillary.
Think about size - what in whole blood is far too big to be squeezed through the tiny gaps between endothelial cells of the capillary wall?
Pick one clear difference, such as large plasma proteins, red blood cells or platelets, and link its absence to being unable to pass through the wall under pressure.
walkthrough:
Identify Fluid R**
Fluid R is tissue fluid. At the arteriole end of the capillary, high hydrostatic pressure forces water, ions, glucose, amino acids and small solutes out through gaps between endothelial cells. Large structures stay behind.

State One Valid Difference**
A safe difference is proteins and cells. Tissue fluid contains no red blood cells, no platelets and no large plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen. It has far fewer proteins overall than blood plasma.

Explain by Size Exclusion**
Red blood cells, platelets and large plasma proteins are too large to fit through the gaps between endothelial cells. Only small molecules are ultrafiltered out under pressure, so they are left behind in the blood. The same logic works for gases if you choose them: tissue fluid has more carbon dioxide from respiring cells and less oxygen than incoming blood.

Final answer: difference: fluid R / tissue fluid has no large plasma proteins / fewer proteins and no red blood cells / no platelets / no white blood cells; explanation: these cells and large proteins are too large to pass through gaps between endothelial cells when fluid is forced out under hydrostatic pressure.

hints: Picture the membrane as two rows facing each other - think about which part loves water and must face the watery cytoplasm and tissue fluid outside.
Zoom in on a single phospholipid - recall how many water-loving heads and water-fearing tails each one has and which way they point in each row.
walkthrough:
Build the Bilayer Framework**
Draw two lines of phospholipids back-to-back. The round phosphate heads point outwards - upper row heads point up toward tissue fluid, lower row heads point down toward cytoplasm - because heads are hydrophilic. The wavy tails point inwards toward each other because tails are hydrophobic and avoid water.

Show Correct Phospholipid Detail**
Each single phospholipid must have exactly one head circle and two tail lines. That 1-head-2-tails pattern repeated in two opposite-facing rows earns full credit for the fluid mosaic bilayer core.

Final answer: Two parallel rows forming a bilayer with hydrophilic phosphate heads pointing outwards and hydrophobic fatty acid tails pointing inwards; each phospholipid shown with one circular head and two wavy tails.

hints: Think about what happens to fatty acid tails when temperature changes - they can pack too tightly when cold or move too much when hot.
walkthrough:
Regulating Fluidity and Stability**
Cholesterol sits tucked among the fatty acid tails. It stops tails packing too closely in the cold, keeping fluidity, and restrains movement in heat, preventing too much fluidity. This keeps the membrane stable but flexible and helps block unwanted hydrophilic ions from leaking through.
Final answer: maintains / regulates fluidity of the membrane and provides mechanical stability, also reduces permeability to hydrophilic substances / ions.

hints: Remember nicotine is a stimulant that activates the sympathetic system - think what that does to how fast and hard the heart beats.
Now think about blood vessels and blood stickiness - what change in vessel diameter and platelet behaviour would raise pressure and clot risk?
walkthrough:
Stimulation of Heart and Vessels**
Nicotine stimulates adrenaline release. The heart beats faster and more strongly, and arterioles constrict. Both effects raise blood pressure in the short term and reduce flow to extremities.

Increased Clotting Risk**
Nicotine also makes platelets stickier, so blood clots more easily, and can damage the endothelium lining. Any two of increased heart rate, increased blood pressure / vasoconstriction, platelet stickiness or endothelial damage give the two marks.
Final answer: increases heart rate; increases blood pressure / causes vasoconstriction / reduces blood flow to extremities; makes platelets sticky / promotes blood clotting; damages endothelium.

hints: Look carefully at Fig. 2.2 arrows - which substance is going down its gradient to power the other substance going up its gradient, and what protein couples them?
Recall sucrose loading into companion cells - what ion gradient is also used there and in which direction does that ion move relative to sucrose?
Compare the direction of $H^+$ movement in the two systems - in Fig. 2.2 $H^+$ leaves the cell, but where does $H^+$ come from when sucrose enters from the apoplast?
walkthrough:
Spot the Shared Secondary Active Mechanism**
Both systems are co-transport, a form of secondary active transport. A single co-transporter protein couples two movements: $H^+$ ions flow down their concentration gradient, releasing energy that drives the other solute - nicotine here, sucrose in phloem - against its concentration gradient into the cytoplasm.

State Similarities Clearly**
So you can state: both involve a co-transport protein, both involve $H^+$ / hydrogen ions / protons, and in both $H^+$ go down the gradient while the coupled solute goes up its gradient. Any two similarities earn up to two marks.

Contrast the Direction of $H^+$ Flow**
The key difference is direction. In Fig. 2.2, $H^+$ move out of the cell from cytoplasm to blood plasma while nicotine moves in. In phloem loading, $H^+$ move into the companion cell from the apoplast / cell wall together with sucrose. The $H^+$ gradient itself is first set up by ATP-driven proton pumps.

Final answer: similarities: both use a co-transport protein; both involve $H^+$ / protons; $H^+$ move down concentration gradient to provide energy for nicotine / sucrose to move against its concentration gradient; differences: in nicotine transport $H^+$ move out of the cell, in sucrose transport $H^+$ move into the cell from apoplast / cell wall.
